planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in full sun on a raised mound in well-drained soil; protect from frost for the first several winters.

directions: A reliable late-season Florida dooryard cultivar with deep red-blushed fruit and a compact, disease-tolerant growth habit. Sets fruit even in cooler, wetter years when other cultivars fail, making it a staple in home orchards along the Gulf Coast. Fruit matures from late summer into fall, later than most commercial cultivars. Give trees room to develop their naturally rounded canopy and avoid overhead irrigation during flowering.
sources: UF/IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden mango variety records

planting.note: Grow in full sun with excellent drainage; this Thai cultivar tolerates containers and heavy pruning better than most mangoes.

directions: A Thai cultivar prized for producing sweet, fiberless fruit that can be eaten green and crunchy or allowed to ripen fully golden. Precocious and heavy-bearing, it often flowers and fruits multiple times a year in warm climates, making it popular with container and greenhouse growers. Keep roots restricted somewhat to encourage the compact growth this cultivar is known for. Thin excess fruit clusters to improve size.
sources: UF/IFAS Tropical Research and Education Center
California Rare Fruit Growers (CRFG) mango notes

planting.note: A naturally dwarf tree suited to small Gulf Coast yards and large containers; plant in full sun with a raised, well-drained bed.

directions: A small, dense Florida dooryard cultivar known for consistent production of sweet, small-to-medium fruit on a compact frame. Its naturally short stature makes it one of the easier mangoes to manage, prune, or cover during cold events. Disease pressure from anthracnose is relatively low compared to larger-fruited cultivars. Ideal as an entry mango for growers with limited space.
sources: UF/IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden mango variety records

planting.note: Well suited to container culture; grow in full sun with acidic, well-drained soil and consistent moisture.

directions: A naturally dwarf lychee cultivar that bears at a small size, making it a favorite among South Florida and Hawaii collectors with limited growing space. Fruit is small but sweet, with a notably thin seed that gives more edible flesh per fruit than many standard cultivars. Its compact habit makes it one of the few lychees practical for long-term container growing or greenhouse protection. Keep soil consistently moist but never waterlogged.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers (CRFG) lychee notes
UF/IFAS Tropical Fruit Program

planting.note: Plant in full sun with acidic, well-drained soil; this cultivar tolerates a wider range of chill accumulation than most lychees.

directions: An Australian-selected cultivar known for a precocious, reliable bearing habit and good fruit quality even where winters are too mild for traditional Chinese cultivars. Widely planted in Queensland orchards and increasingly found in Florida and California collector groves seeking dependable production. Fruit is medium-sized with a pleasant balance of sweetness and acidity. Responds well to light annual pruning to maintain a manageable, productive canopy.
sources: CRFG lychee variety records
Queensland DPI lychee cultivar trials

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; longan tolerates slightly cooler winters than lychee but still needs frost protection when young.

directions: A Hawaii-developed longan cultivar selected for consistent bearing and good fruit size in warm, humid lowland conditions. Flesh is sweet and aromatic with the characteristic musky-sweet longan flavor, and the tree tends to bear more reliably than many seedling trees. Performs well where mild winters limit chill-dependent fruiting of other cultivars. Thin heavy fruit clusters to improve individual fruit size.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR fruit crop records
CRFG longan variety notes

planting.note: Plant in full sun with well-drained soil; hand-pollinate flowers in the evening or early morning to ensure good fruit set.

directions: An older Florida atemoya cultivar grown for its smooth, custardy flesh and good flavor on a compact, manageable tree. Like other atemoyas it benefits greatly from hand pollination because its natural pollinators are scarce outside its native range. Fruit ripens over a long season, extending the harvest window beyond many single-flush cultivars. Prune annually to keep the canopy open and fruit within easy reach for hand-pollination and picking.
sources: Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates
CRFG atemoya/cherimoya variety notes

planting.note: Needs a cooler, drier climate than true tropical fruit; plant in full sun with excellent drainage and hand-pollinate for reliable fruit set.

directions: A long-cultivated Southern California cherimoya selection valued for good-flavored fruit and reasonable productivity under the cool coastal conditions cherimoyas prefer over humid tropical heat. One of the older named cultivars still referenced alongside Booth, Whaley, and Pierce in California collector circles. Hand pollination with a soft brush is usually necessary where natural pollinators are absent. Harvest when fruit begins to soften slightly and the skin color lightens.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers (CRFG) cherimoya Fruit Facts

planting.note: Grow in full sun with cool nights and excellent drainage; hand pollination improves fruit set substantially.

directions: An older California cherimoya cultivar grown for smooth-skinned fruit with creamy, mild flavor, historically listed alongside Chaffey and McPherson in Southern California collector plantings. Prefers the dry, mild-winter climate of coastal California over humid Gulf Coast heat, making it a better fit for greenhouse or arid-microclimate growers. Fruit develops over several months and should be harvested while still firm, then ripened indoors at room temperature. Protect from both hard frost and prolonged summer humidity.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers (CRFG) cherimoya Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant in full sun or light shade on well-drained soil; young trees need frost protection for the first few winters.

directions: An older Florida carambola cultivar grown historically for its heavy, reliable fruit set and tangy, more acidic flavor than modern sweet-type cultivars like Arkin. Its tart fruit is well suited to cooking, juicing, and preserves rather than fresh eating out of hand. A dependable bearer across multiple flowering flushes each year in warm climates. Thin crowded fruit clusters to reduce limb breakage on young wood.
sources: Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates
UF/IFAS Tropical Fruit Program

planting.note: Plant in full sun on well-drained soil; mulch well and protect young trees from frost and strong wind.

directions: A tart-fruited Florida carambola cultivar from the same era as Newcomb and Golden Star, grown mainly for cooking and juice rather than fresh eating. Vigorous and productive, it was once common in older Miami-Dade dooryard plantings before sweet-type cultivars became dominant in the nursery trade. The waxy, deeply ribbed fruit holds up well to processing. Give the tree consistent moisture during fruit development to reduce premature drop.
sources: Julia Morton, Fruits of Warm Climates
UF/IFAS Tropical Fruit Program
